preference_rationale: B is much more tractable, and overall more practical for this desk. A tries to kill the circularity, which is the right instinct, but falters on the alternate valuation metric it adopts to do it. B answers the question as asked and returns something a PM can size with - per-industry elasticities expressed in turns of multiple, with an out-of-sample quintile sort behind them.
critique_A:
Killing the circularity is good, but the fix falters. EV/LTM EBITDA is not how assets are priced in public markets - pricing is mostly on forward earnings, not prior earnings - so A trades a mechanical problem for a measure that does not reflect the thing being studied.

TAQ data makes absolutely zero sense for this project. The time horizon for a multiple re-rating is months to years, not milliseconds. (This desk also has no tick data, but the horizon mismatch is the real objection and would stand at any firm.)

A gates on the seed's question and then spends the project on two others - regime stability and re-rating efficiency. Those are legitimate questions, but the elasticity itself is the deliverable here and A never produces a usable one.

Near-zero and negative EBITDA denominators are handled by screening them out (margin >= 2%). The natural fix is to switch to a revenue multiple rather than drop the observations.
critique_B:
B should be able to solve the circularity properly rather than decompose around it: make the independent variable backward-looking (realized CAGR) and the dependent variable forward-looking. The EV identity decomposition is a workaround, not a fix.

Log multiples do not make sense in this case.

The negative-denominator problem is handled by screening to NTM and N2Y EBITDA > 0, which drops exactly the firm-quarters where re-rating is most violent. Switching to a revenue multiple handles those cases instead of excluding them.

Neither plan addresses the metric shifting as a company matures - revenue for high-growth, EBITDA for mature. B has revenue CAGR as a second regressor and EV/Sales as an alternate dependent variable, but never models the transition.
why_loser_was_defensible: A is the only one of the two that confronts the circularity head-on and removes it by construction rather than decomposing around it, and its event-study identification off single-broker revisions on off-cycle days is genuinely cleaner. An analyst who ranked identification above measure realism would have taken A.
